title: The Letter from Hogwarts
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 35 of 40
content:
The Board of Governors offered Snape his job back in April.

Sort of.

The letter was six pages long and contained enough conditions to qualify as architecture.

He could return as Potions Master.

He could reclaim Slytherin House if McGonagall agreed.

He would be subject to classroom observation for one year.

Former-student complaints could be reviewed by a conduct committee.

Corporal punishment was prohibited, which made Snape write in the margin: WAS IT NOT BEFORE?

Public disparagement of students was prohibited.

He read that line twice.

Then set the letter down.

I did not make a joke.

“Do you want it?” I asked.

Snape stared at the fire.

“I wanted that job before you were born.”

“Probably.”

His eyes narrowed.

I smiled faintly.

He had been teaching Potions since he was barely out of school himself, too young for the authority he carried, trapped in a role that served Dumbledore's strategy as much as any educational purpose.

“What do you want now?” I asked.

“That is an irritatingly different question.”

“Yes.”

He picked up the letter.

The fountain pen I gave him lay beside it.

“I miss the laboratory.”

“You have a laboratory.”

“I miss this laboratory.”

The Hogwarts dungeon.

The room he had ruled, damaged, protected, slept beside, returned to.

“I miss teaching advanced students who are not idiots.”

“How many is that?”

“Historically? Three.”

“Generous.”

His mouth twitched.

“I do not miss first years.”

“No?”

“They melt things.”

“You terrified them.”

“They still melted things.”

“Maybe because they were terrified.”

His expression soured.

“Perhaps.”

The word was important.

He read the conduct clause again.

“Could you teach differently?” I asked.

Snape looked at me.

“Do not ask whether I would.”

“I didn't.”

“You asked whether I could.”

“Yes.”

He leaned back.

“I do not know.”

There it was again.

A phrase he once seemed physically incapable of saying.

I smiled.

“Why are you pleased?”

“You admitted uncertainty.”

“I do so regularly.”

“You once argued with a thermometer.”

“It was poorly calibrated.”

“It agreed with me.”

“Exactly.”

He looked away to hide a smile.

The letter remained on the desk for a week.

During that week, Snape did something unexpected.

He observed classes.

Not officially.

He stood at the back of Professor Slughorn's Potions lessons twice. Slughorn had returned temporarily to help Hogwarts through the transition and treated Snape's presence with forced cheerfulness.

I attended one lesson from the adjoining prep room.

A second-year melted a ladle.

Snape's entire body reacted.

I covered my mouth.

He glared through the glass.

Slughorn rescued the potion, laughed, and explained the mistake without humiliating the student.

Snape watched.

Not approvingly.

Not dismissively either.

After class, he said, “He wastes time.”

“He kept the student from crying.”

“Crying is not fatal.”

“No. But neither is patience.”

His eyes narrowed.

Then the student returned.

The small boy stood at the door clutching the repaired ladle.

“Professor Snape?”

Snape went still.

“Not presently.”

“My dad had you.”

“Condolences.”

The boy smiled uncertainly.

“He said you knew everything about antidotes.”

“That is an exaggeration.”

“Can you tell me why mine went orange?”

Snape looked at me.

I raised my eyebrows.

He looked back at the boy.

“What did you add before the bezoar extract?”

“Lavender.”

“How much?”

“A spoon.”

“What size spoon?”

The boy held up the ladle.

Snape closed his eyes.

I bit my lip.

When he opened them, he did not insult the child.

He said, “The recipe means a standard measure, not whatever object is currently in your hand.”

The boy's ears turned red.

Snape noticed.

His jaw tightened.

Then he added, “The terminology is poorly explained in the text. I will show you.”

He took the boy to the measurement cabinet.

I stood in the doorway, stunned.

Snape glanced back.

“Do not,” he said.

I smiled.

“I said nothing.”

“Your face is intolerable.”

The boy looked between us.

“Are you two married?”

Silence.

Snape looked as though he had been struck by a Stunning Spell.

I choked.

“No,” I said.

The boy nodded. “My mum looks at my dad like that.”

Snape turned scarlet.

“Class dismissed,” he said.

“I'm not in class.”

“Leave.”

The boy left, delighted.

I leaned against the cabinet, laughing.

“I hate children,” Snape said.

“No, you don't.”

“I am reconsidering the profession.”

“You just taught him without making him cry.”

“A low standard.”

“Low standards have served me well.”

He glared.

That evening, Snape read the Board letter again.

Then he took out his pen.

I sat across from him.

“What are you writing?”

“A counteroffer.”

My eyebrows rose.

He wrote for twenty minutes.

When he finished, he handed it to me.

He would not return as full-time Potions Master.

He would accept a part-time advanced seminar for N.E.W.T.-level students, a research appointment, and responsibility for curriculum review.

He would not resume Head of Slytherin.

He requested explicit student complaint procedures and classroom observation not only for himself but for all staff.

I looked up.

“Everyone?”

“If oversight is educationally valuable, it should not be used as theater for one controversial teacher.”

“That is annoyingly reasonable.”

“I know.”

“Are you sure?”

Snape looked toward the dungeon classroom.

“No.”

Then he signed the letter.

“But I would like to try.”

It was the answer I hoped for.

Not return.

Not escape.

Try.\n\nThe signature did not end the argument.\n\nIt started a new one.\n\n“You cannot simply sign their terms unchanged,” I said.\n\nSnape looked up from the parchment. “I have just done precisely that.”\n\n“You wrote three objections in the margins.”\n\n“Observations.”\n\n“One says, ‘This clause was clearly drafted by someone who has never entered a classroom.’”\n\n“An observation.”\n\n“Another says, ‘Define public disparagement.’”\n\n“A necessary legal clarification.”\n\n“The third just says, ‘No.’”\n\n“The clearest of the three.”\n\nI pulled the letter toward me. “If you're going back because you want to teach differently, make them give you conditions you can actually follow.”\n\nHis eyes narrowed. “You propose I negotiate for stricter oversight?”\n\n“I propose you negotiate for useful oversight.”\n\n“That sounds suspiciously like governance.”\n\n“Terrible, I know.”\n\nSnape stared at the fire.\n\nThen, slowly, he took a fresh sheet of parchment.\n\n“What would you change?” he asked.\n\nI tried not to look too pleased.\n\n“First, classroom observation should include feedback, not just surveillance.”\n\nHe wrote.\n\n“Second, student complaints need a process that doesn't require a terrified eleven-year-old to argue with the professor they're complaining about.”\n\nHis quill paused.\n\n“Reasonable.”\n\n“Third, you need the right to remove a student from dangerous practical work immediately.”\n\n“That was never in question.”\n\n“Put it in writing anyway.”\n\nHe did.\n\n“Fourth—”\n\n“There is a fourth?”\n\n“You should have an assistant for first-year practicals.”\n\n“No.”\n\n“You said you wanted fewer melted things.”\n\n“I said first years melt things. I did not say I wished to multiply first years by adding another incompetent person.”\n\n“Hire a competent one.”\n\n“Where?”\n\nI smiled.\n\nHis eyes narrowed. “Absolutely not.”\n\n“I didn't say me.”\n\n“You thought it.”\n\n“Very loudly?”\n\n“Deafeningly.”\n\nI laughed. “Fine. Not me. I have my own work.”\n\nSomething in his expression eased.\n\nThat mattered.\n\nThe old version of this relationship—if it could have existed at all—might have asked one of us to disappear into the other person's life. I did not want that. I wanted a life large enough for both of us to keep choosing it.\n\nSnape added a final paragraph requesting a formal review at the end of the first term rather than after a full year.\n\n“If I am failing,” he said, “there is no reason to wait twelve months to establish it.”\n\n“And if you're doing well?”\n\n“Then Minerva may enjoy telling the Board they worried unnecessarily.”\n\n“She will enjoy that.”\n\n“Excessively.”\n\nHe sanded the parchment.\n\nI read the draft once.\n\nIt was sharp. Defensive in places. Practical everywhere. It did not promise that Severus Snape had transformed into a gentle man with endless patience. It promised something more believable: that he would accept accountability, change specific behaviors, protect students from danger, and remain himself while doing it.\n\n“Send that one,” I said.\n\nHe looked at the signed original.\n\nThen tore it neatly in half.\n\nThe sound was small and satisfying.\n\nAn owl left the dungeon that afternoon carrying the counterproposal.\n\nFor three days, Snape pretended not to care whether the Board accepted it.\n\nOn the first day he reorganized the antidote cabinet.\n\nOn the second he rewrote a lesson plan for a class he did not technically have.\n\nOn the third he asked me, with elaborate casualness, whether I thought a first-year student should be permitted to handle powdered bicorn horn.\n\n“No.”\n\n“Good.”\n\n“Are you planning classes?”\n\n“No.”\n\n“You're holding a syllabus.”\n\n“This is unrelated.”\n\n“Of course.”\n\nThe reply arrived the next morning.\n\nSnape stood in the doorway with the Board's seal broken beneath his thumb.\n\n“Well?” I asked.\n\nHis face gave me nothing.\n\nThen he handed me the parchment.\n\nAcross the top, in Minerva's severe handwriting, someone had written:\n\nACCEPTED, WITH THREE AMENDMENTS.\n\nI looked up.\n\nSnape sighed as if the universe had personally inconvenienced him by offering a future.\n\n“Apparently,” he said, “I am going back.”
